Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: Diego Reyes had been seventeen when he deployed to the valley, a young corporal on foot patrol when the ridge erupted in dust and rifle fire. He remembered the exact moment the earth cracked beneath his boots, the sharp crack of a round passing close enough to singe his uniform, and the way his squad mate had folded without a sound. In the months that followed, those moments refused to settle into the background. They arrived more real than normal, pressing against his mind with the same weight and texture as the present. When he closed his eyes, he could feel the heat of the desert sun and hear the static of his radio. If he thought of his comrade collapsing, a hot wave of rage would surge through his chest, sudden and unyielding, though Diego had come to accept it as simply what happened when the past refused to stay past. Returning home brought a quiet street and a still apartment, yet Diego could not relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. He lay awake listening to the floorboards settle, his shoulders locked, convinced that trouble could still arrive. Ordinary sounds—a car door shutting, a chair scraping, the heavy thud of a camera lens clicking into place—made him startle, his breath catching mid-draw. He had stopped taking unnecessary risks, or perhaps he had started moving through intersections with a reckless certainty, never pausing to look up. Sometimes, without warning, a flicker of hallway light or the smell of dust would pull the full memory back, and he would find himself standing very still in his parents’ kitchen, waiting for a threat that never quite materialized. His work as a photographer became the concrete ground where his days unfolded. Diego spent his hours in a cramped studio overlooking the street, adjusting tripods, framing shots, and watching his subjects through the viewfinder. He had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that their easy laughter and familiar nods hid a reliability he could no longer count on. When his assistant once dropped a reflector near the worktable, Diego felt a sharp, quiet distrust rise in his throat, while beside it sat the unshaken conviction that he should have protected his comrade on that ridge. The two thoughts rested together, neither prompting the other, as he continued to lower his camera and step back from the edge of his own lens. Over the weeks and months, his habits hardened. He stopped walking past the old community center, and he began carrying his camera everywhere, a familiar weight that felt like armor. He avoided letting anyone else handle his equipment, and his studio work slowed as he turned away from crowded photoshoots. He missed his sister’s graduation, and the hall’s echoing footsteps stayed with him, mirroring the boots on gravel. His mother noticed how he moved through the house, how he checked the windows and adjusted the locks, how he worked late in his darkroom until the red light felt like the only safe color. He had come to believe he belonged nowhere, caught between the dust of the valley and the quiet of his suburban street. A PCL-5 score of 77 mirrored the quiet intensity of his days. What frightened him most was not the past returning, but the present slipping away while he waited for it to break. When his camera finally needed repair and he realized he could no longer bear the silence of his empty apartment, Diego scheduled an appointment. The appointment card sat on his desk beside his developing tray, a quiet invitation he was ready to accept. He hoped to find a way to step out of the waiting room and into the world, carrying his memories without letting them pull him under.
